explanations.answer: Whether he will recover from this illness
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Ben-hadad, king of Aram, tells his man Hazael to inquire of the LORD through Elisha, the prophet from Israel: "Will I recover from this illness?" (2 Kings 8:8). When you're sick, that's the only question in your head. Everything else can wait in line.

Good guess if you were thinking about kings and armies, friend. But the text doesn't have the king asking about Israel at all. Ben-hadad, king of Aram, is sick, and his question is about that illness: "Will I recover from this illness?" (2 Kings 8:8).

explanations.answer: Who will reign over Aram after him
explanations.explanation: I see where that comes from, since the man asking is a king. But Ben-hadad, king of Aram, sends Hazael with a question about his own health. He wants to know, "Will I recover from this illness?" (2 Kings 8:8). A sick man asks about getting better first.

Yes, those are the words Elisha, the LORD's prophet in Israel, gives Hazael to carry back: "Go and tell him, ‘You will surely recover.’…" Hazael, the king's man, hears that and probably thinks the news is good. But hold on, because Elisha isn't done. Keep reading the very next line, friend.

That sounds like something a nervous doctor would say, but Elisha, the prophet from Israel, never says it. He tells Hazael, the king's man, to go and say, "You will surely recover." The answer is short and clear (2 Kings 8:10). The twist comes right after it.

Nope, Elisha never says a word about a divided kingdom here. Hazael, the king's man, asked about the king's illness, so the message is about the illness. Elisha, the prophet from Israel, says to tell Ben-hadad, "You will surely recover." (2 Kings 8:10).

That's what Elisha says next. First he tells Hazael to say the king will recover, "But the LORD has shown me that in fact he will die." (2 Kings 8:10). Two messages in one breath, friend. I think that's a lot for Hazael to carry back down the road.

Fleeing isn't in the text, friend. Elisha, the LORD's prophet in Israel, says that the LORD has shown him Ben-hadad, king of Aram, "will die." (2 Kings 8:10). Nobody is fleeing anywhere in that sentence.

I get why that one tempts, but Elisha doesn't say it here. He tells Hazael, the king's man, that the LORD has shown him that the king "will die." (2 Kings 8:10). Nothing is said about Ben-hadad, king of Aram, repenting in these verses.

Yes, the man of God begins to weep (2 Kings 8:11). That's after Elisha fixes his gaze steadily on Hazael, the king's man, until Hazael becomes uncomfortable. A prophet staring is one thing, but a prophet staring and then crying is a whole different level. I'd have a lot of questions too.

Laughing would have been a strange way to end that stare, wouldn't it? The text says Elisha, the prophet from Israel, "…began to weep." (2 Kings 8:11). Hazael, the king's man, is already uncomfortable, and tears make it even more serious.

I like the optimism, friend, but nobody breaks into song here. After Elisha, the LORD's prophet in Israel, holds his gaze on Hazael, the king's man, the text says he "…began to weep." (2 Kings 8:11). No music for this moment.

explanations.answer: He knows the evil Hazael will do to Israel
explanations.explanation: That's exactly what Elisha says. Hazael asks, "Why is my lord weeping?" and Elisha, the LORD's prophet in Israel, answers, "Because I know the evil you will do to the Israelites…" (2 Kings 8:12). The tears are for what's coming to Israel's people, and I think we can sit quietly with that for a moment.

explanations.answer: He misses his home and family in Israel
explanations.explanation: That's a tender guess, friend, but the text gives a different reason. Elisha, the prophet from Israel, tells Hazael, the king's man, "Because I know the evil you will do to the Israelites…" (2 Kings 8:12). When the Bible states the reason, we keep it.

explanations.answer: He cannot accept such a large gift
explanations.explanation: Forty camel loads is a LOT of gift, I'll give you that. But Elisha, the prophet from Israel, never mentions the gift when Hazael, the king's man, asks why he's weeping. His answer is, "Because I know the evil you will do to the Israelites…" (2 Kings 8:12).

Yes, Hazael, the king's man, hears all of it and asks, "But how could your servant, a mere dog, do such a monstrous thing?" (2 Kings 8:13). He calls himself a mere dog, and he calls the deed monstrous. It's a heavy moment in the passage. Elisha, the LORD's prophet in Israel, answers with something else the LORD has shown him.

The text says the opposite. Hazael, the king's man, does ask: "But how could your servant, a mere dog, do such a monstrous thing?" (2 Kings 8:13). So he doesn't stay quiet when Elisha, the prophet from Israel, tells him what's ahead. This part is heavy, so it's worth reading slowly.

explanations.answer: Hazael will be king over Aram
explanations.explanation: That's it. Elisha, the LORD's prophet in Israel, answers, "The LORD has shown me that you will be king over Aram." (2 Kings 8:13). Hazael, the king's man, asked how he could ever do such a thing, and the answer is this news about a crown. A servant carrying camel loads just got told he's going to wear the crown.

explanations.answer: Hazael will fall in battle soon
explanations.explanation: That's not what Elisha says, friend. When Hazael, the king's man, asks how he could do such a thing, Elisha, the prophet from Israel, answers, "The LORD has shown me that you will be king over Aram." (2 Kings 8:13). The text points to a throne, and there's no battle in his answer.

Interesting guess, but no. Elisha, the LORD's prophet in Israel, says nothing about Hazael becoming a prophet. He tells Hazael, the king's man, "The LORD has shown me that you will be king over Aram." (2 Kings 8:13). Hazael is headed for a throne.

Careful here, friend, because the text says something else. When Ben-hadad, king of Aram, asks what Elisha said, Hazael replies, "He told me that you would surely recover." (2 Kings 8:14). He doesn't pass on the part about the king dying. Elisha did say it to Hazael (2 Kings 8:10), but the king didn't hear it from him.

Right, this one is false. Ben-hadad, king of Aram, asks Hazael what Elisha said, and Hazael answers, "He told me that you would surely recover." (2 Kings 8:14). Elisha had also said the LORD showed him the king would die (2 Kings 8:10), but that part isn't in Hazael's answer. The very next day, things move fast.
